newsitem.title: FRANCE: Albania president says country calm, stable.
newsitem.headline: Albania president says country calm, stable.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha has accused his opponents of trying to turn protests over the collapse of investment schemes into a bloodbath but said the government would maintain political and economic stability.
"The opposition made a big mistake. It wanted a bloodbath and it did not happen," Berisha told the French daily Le Monde in an interview published on Thursday.

"Albania is calm," he said. But as the interview was published, tens of thousands of demonstrators demanding his resignation swept through lines of riot police to occupy the centre of the southern Albanian city of Vlore in a second day of protests.
Berisha said "fanatic ex-Communists" had jumped on the bandwagon of protests by small investors ruined by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.
"They believed the time had come to use violence to overthrow the government. They were wrong," he said.

The main opposition groups joined forces last week in a "Forum for Democracy" to press for the resignation of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi, but the alliance lacks a charismatic leader and is perceived to be deeply divided.
Berisha said the opposition boycotted two invitations for talks this week, but he would continue to seek negotiations.
"I will keep on doing my best to pull the opposition out of the spiral of conspiracy in which it lives," he said.
"There will be no economic or political instability. We are going to identify those who lost the most. We will not abandon them in misfortune," Berisha said.
He denied the government had backed the investment companies and said some were foes of his Democratic Party.
"If the government were involved, it would not have a free hand. But it has a free hand," he said.
Virtually every family has invested money in the schemes in the six years since Albania emerged from eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime.
Some accuse the Democratic Party, founded by Berisha, of using the proceeds to finance its re-election in polls last year, denounced as rigged by Western observers.

A small number of other investment schemes are clinging to life. Local economists, who believe as much as $2 billion was tied up in all the schemes, say the collapse of other companies is inevitable and could pitch Albania into uncontrollable violence.
